title: US nursing-home mergers reduce deficiency citations but also reduce direct-care hours without improving resident health
source_unit: US nursing-home chain mergers, facility quality citations, direct-care hours, marginal cost, and resident health outcomes

observations.period: Working paper issued June 2025; revised July 2026; facility-level data from 1999–2019

denominator.unit: US nursing-home facilities acquired by chains and comparison facilities; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

deficiency_citations.unit: percent change in health deficiency citations in the three years after acquisition

persistence.unit: years for which the reduction in deficiency citations persists

citation_severity.unit: citation reduction is concentrated in low-severity categories

resident_health.unit: no meaningful impact of mergers on residents’ health outcomes

cost_efficiency.unit: a structural model attributes the citation decline to reductions in marginal costs of serving residents

observations.method: Facility-level staggered difference-in-differences estimates compare acquired nursing homes with comparison facilities; a structural model examines marginal costs and the proposed mechanism.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose facility counts, effect sizes beyond the 8% citation estimate, exact health outcomes, or all identification assumptions. The estimate is a working-paper result; citation reduction, direct-care hours, and resident health are distinct units and should not be collapsed into one quality measure.
observations.subgroup: Acquired facilities, with stronger reported citation effects in cross-market mergers and mergers involving smaller or low-deficiency chains.
observations.counterinterpretation: Acquisition selection, reporting, inspection behavior, staffing mix, resident composition, payer mix, and facility exit can affect post-merger measures; fewer citations may represent compliance or measurement change rather than better clinical care, while the reported direct-care-hour decline may vary by facility and worker category.

related_sources.claim: Nursing homes respond strategically to inspections, and higher ratings predict relative mortality despite weak absolute-quality interpretation.
California nursing homes manipulate size around a 100-bed staffing threshold, limiting access particularly for disadvantaged patients.
Detailed nursing-home financial evidence reports widespread related-party tunneling and a gap between reported and implied investment returns.

boundary: This record adds an ownership and compliance-versus-care comparison to the US nursing-home chain. It does not establish that mergers improve or worsen overall quality, and it does not measure worker voice, prices, profits, resident experience, access, or long-run health in the same unit.
